description:
We're OrbiNivra, a team of curious and motivated students from Ben Guerir, Morocco, who love exploring new ideas and solving real-world problems.

We're passionate about AI, technology, and using NASA data to make a positive impact. We believe great ideas come from teamwork, creativity, and learning from each other.

We're looking for enthusiastic people interested in coding, data science, AI, design, or Earth observation.
summary: At the lunar south pole, the region targeted by upcoming crewed and robotic missions, the Sun skims the horizon and Earth hangs low, so a few hundred metres or a few days decide whether a lander can touch down safely, make power and talk to Earth. Sightline finds the best places to land for a given mission. The user enters when the mission starts, how long it lasts and which landing system flies (compact, medium, heavy, shadow-capable or custom tolerances). In a few seconds Sightline screens 14,884 candidate spots in four regions hour by hour over the mission period (sunlight, line of sight to Earth, slope, roughness, relief, obstacles), re-analyses the best ones on NASA LOLA laser altimetry at 80 m, and returns three admissible sites at least 2 km apart. Each site comes with a transparent Landing Complexity (%): eliminatory constraints are kept separate from eight weighted complexity factors, each normalised by the lander's own tolerance, with the main drivers and the data completeness shown. It is a screening difficulty index, never a success probability. A full-screen 3D Moon shows the sites on real LRO imagery down to about 1 m per pixel, with heatmaps of slope, complexity, sunlight and Earth link. Sun and Earth positions come from JPL DE440 via NAIF SPICE and are validated against JPL Horizons to 2.7e-5 degrees. Results export as a PDF report, JSON, CSV or a shareable link. Free, static, in English and French.
details:
THE PROBLEM

At the lunar south pole the Sun skims the horizon and Earth wobbles near it, so a few hundred metres or a few days change everything: whether the lander can touch down, make power and talk to Earth. The data exists (LOLA, LROC, Moon Trek, Horizons), but comparing many site, date and lander combinations quickly is hard for non-specialists.

WHAT SIGHTLINE DOES

- Find sites (default page), three steps. Configure: mission start date and duration in days (the end date is computed and inclusive: a 1-day mission ends the day it starts), landing-system profile, optional custom tolerances (maximum slope, landing-ellipse radius, minimum usable area, minimum sunlight, longest night, minimum Earth link). Analyze: a progress view while a Web Worker screens every candidate and refines the best 40 per region on 80 m terrain. Top 3: three sites with Landing Complexity (Low / Moderate / High), mission compatibility, surface suitability, reasons and a watch-out; side-by-side comparison; a map of the Top 3 on LOLA relief; why the other spots were excluded; a detail view per site (80 m relief map, factor breakdown, requirements checked, figures over the period, sources, what to verify) with links to the 3D view, the expert workbench and LROC QuickMap. Fewer than three admissible sites are shown as they are, never padded.

- Landing Complexity model. Eight factors, each normalised by the lander tolerance: slope 25%, usable area 15%, roughness, relief, obstacles, stability, touchdown light and touchdown Earth link 10% each. Levels at thirds. Eliminatory constraints (for example slope or sunlight beyond the lander tolerance) exclude a spot instead of adding to its score.

- 3D Moon. Moved like a web map (inertia, zoom to cursor, tilt). NASA Moon Trek imagery sharpens as you zoom: LRO WAC worldwide; at the south pole LRO NAC mosaics to about 4 m per pixel (1 m at Malapert) or LOLA shaded relief to 5 m, on real LOLA terrain, with flat lighting or the true Sun and its shadows. Layers: slope against the lander limit over the polar cap and, for the mission, Landing Complexity, sunlight and Earth link for every candidate, each with a legend. A 3D tour flies over the Top 3.

- Expert workbench. Illumination and power (array layouts, mast heights, battery survival timeline), direct-to-Earth windows with the Deep Space Network, tip-over screening and landing-ellipse Monte Carlo, "who blocks the Sun", scenario comparison, mission replay (IM-1, IM-2, Chandrayaan-3), printable Mission Brief.

- For everyone. Learn mode with a guided tour and glossary, English and French, keyboard operable, colour-blind-safe colour ramps, works offline once loaded, and a 30-page user guide.

HOW WE KNOW IT IS RIGHT

A validation matrix generated from recorded test output (in-app Methods & Trust page): browser ephemeris vs SPICE 2.7e-5 deg; vs 2,012 cached JPL Horizons rows 2.7e-5 deg; Moon elevation at the DSN stations vs Horizons 0.0005 deg; curated horizon masks recomputed from LOLA 80 m match the reference to 0.001 deg; Apollo 11 touchdown Sun elevation 10.703 deg (Horizons 10.703 deg); event times within 0.5 s of a 1 s scan; energy within 3.6e-6 % of a one-minute reference over a year; site finder deterministic, every option within the hard constraints at 80 m and at least 2 km apart; slope heatmap vs the validated plane fit: median 0.16 deg, P90 0.47 deg on 400 LOLA points.

HONEST LIMITS

Terrain is LOLA 80 m (plus 240 m far field): lander-scale rocks and craters (such as the ~20 m crater that tipped IM-2) are below the model's resolution, which the mission replay shows. NAC imagery is displayed for context and does not feed the calculations. No reflected light, thermal or dust effects; landing-system profiles are generic and illustrative. Screening estimates, not certification. Not endorsed by NASA.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js, Web Workers; Python (spiceypy, numpy) for the data pipeline; Vitest, pytest and Playwright with axe accessibility checks.
